summary:
Ingushetia is a republic of Russia and stands under the Russian national framework; the findings below concern conditions documented specifically for the republic and the wider North Caucasus region.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) treats the North Caucasus, including Ingushetia, as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory assessment of Russia. It finds that trans people and public LGBT+ advocates in the region are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution.

The same note documents systematic regional campaigns against LGBT+ people between 2017 and 2024, and states that the November 2023 extremist designation exposes LGBT+ activity in the region to two to six years' imprisonment, rising to six to ten years for organising. It records that the violence associated with these campaigns has spread beyond the region.

Global Affairs Canada advises avoid all travel to Russia and lists Ingushetia among the republics with frequent terrorist attacks, alongside Chechnya, Dagestan and Stavropol Krai. The advisory notes surveillance of foreigners and states that 2SLGBTQI+ persons, their allies and their families have been attacked, harassed and abused. It further notes that organisations advocating for 2SLGBTQI+ issues are treated as extremist since January 2024, and that the Ministry of Interior requires special permission to enter certain areas.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, interviewed by the Human Rights House Foundation, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. He attests that conditions in the region have deteriorated year on year.
tangentialFactors:
The two foreign-government assessments differ in scope. The UK Home Office judges Russia overall as non-persecutory for LGBT+ people and carves out the North Caucasus as the exception, while Global Affairs Canada advises avoid all travel to the country as a whole and separately flags Ingushetia for terrorist attacks. A traveller therefore meets two different framings of the same territory.

The Canadian advisory's grouping of Ingushetia with Chechnya, Dagestan and Stavropol Krai is a list of named jurisdictions with frequent terrorist attacks; it supplies no incident counts, population figures or per-capita rates, so the ordering of that list carries no comparative risk magnitude.

The Home Office's regional finding rests on campaigns documented between 2017 and 2024, with the note published in June 2025; no later regional review is present in this inventory.

The neighbouring republic of Chechnya is where the best-documented North Caucasus purge is recorded: more than 100 men detained and tortured and at least three extrajudicial killings from February 2017, and around 40 detained and two killed in the December 2018 to January 2019 purge, confirmed by a December 2018 OSCE report and followed by March 2021 EU sanctions on two Chechen officials. These figures concern Chechnya, not Ingushetia.

Isteev's statement is an advocate's testimony rather than a measured statistic: deterioration is asserted year on year without counts, and the inventory contains no survey of trans people in the republic.
localsOnly:
David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus, and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. He describes conditions as having worsened each year.

The UK Home Office note records systematic regional campaigns against LGBT+ people between 2017 and 2024, and states that residents who organise face six to ten years' imprisonment under the extremist designation, with participation or repeated display of symbols carrying two to six years.

The Canadian advisory states that 2SLGBTQI+ persons, their allies and their families have been attacked, harassed and abused, and that advocacy organisations have been treated as extremist since January 2024.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Ingushetia-specific prosecution, court ruling, killing or incident is documented in this inventory. The most recent region-specific assessment available here is the UK Home Office note of June 2025; no later regional review is sourced.

The Home Office's reference to systematic campaigns between 2017 and 2024 is stated at North Caucasus level and is not itemised by republic in this inventory, so the share attributable to Ingushetia is unresolved.

No trans-specific violence rate, and no denominator of any kind, is available for the republic; the raw hate-crime totals circulating for Russia as a whole are national counts over 2010 to 2020 and are not attributable to this region.

Whether the national bans on gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been applied to Ingushetia residents specifically, and whether any local registry office or medical facility has refused a resident, is not sourced here.

The Canadian advisory's Ministry of Interior special-permission requirement for certain areas is not specified as to which parts of the republic it covers.
